chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Ahmad ibn al-Nadr, from Abu Ja'far al-Fazari, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) called one of his freed slaves, who was called Musaddif, and gave him one thousand dinars, and said to him, 'Prepare yourself so that you may depart for Egypt, for my dependents have increased.'

So he equipped him with goods, and he departed with the merchants. When they drew near to Egypt, a caravan coming out of Egypt met them, and they asked about the goods they had with them, what their condition was in the city. The goods were those of the general public, so they informed them that there was none of it in Egypt. So they swore an oath and made a contract that they would not reduce the profit of each dinar by a dinar.

When they had collected their money, they returned to the city. So Musaddif entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and with him were two bags, in each of which was one thousand dinars. He said, 'May I be your ransom, this is the principal capital, and this other is the profit.'

He (peace be upon him) said, 'Indeed, this profit is large, but what did you do with the goods?' So he told him how they acted and how they swore an oath. He said, 'Glory be to Allah, you swear upon a people of Muslims that you will not sell to them except with a profit of one dinar per dinar.'

Then he took the bag and said, 'This is my principal capital, and we have no need for this profit.' Then he said, 'O Musaddif, the dueling of swords is lighter/easier than seeking the halal (permissible livelihood).'

key_terms.بِرِبْحِ الدِّينَارِ دِينَارًا: With a profit of one dinar per dinar (guaranteed doubling)
key_terms.تَحَالَفُوا: They swore an oath (to a common goal)
key_terms.مُصَادِفٌ: Musaddif, a freed slave of the Imam

ai.seo_question: What is the story of Musaddif and the Imam's lesson on trade ethics?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic distinction between legitimate trade and *gharar* (uncertainty) or market manipulation, where merchants conspired to withhold goods to guarantee profit. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) accepted the principal but rejected the excessive profit derived from this artificial scarcity, highlighting that securing a lawful livelihood through such deceptive practices is more arduous than physical combat. This narrative serves as a practical ethical guideline for merchants to avoid exploitative market behaviors that distort fair value.
